objection: Didn’t Jesus say, ‘The Father is greater than I’—and call him the only true God?
answer:
Both texts describe real facts, but not the fact the objection needs. John 14:28 speaks within the economy of the incarnation: the Son, having taken the form of a servant, is on mission from the Father, and a sent son can rightly call the sender "greater" in respect of that order without being of a lesser nature. The Father-Son relation itself involves an order of origin — the Son eternally begotten of the Father — without implying inequality of essence, just as a human son shares his father's full humanity despite originating from him. John 17:3 likewise distinguishes the Father and Son personally, but distinguishing persons is not excluding one from the divine identity; Jesus has just asked to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world existed, hardly the request of a mere exalted creature.

And this is exactly why we can't read these two verses in isolation from the Gospel that contains them: the same John who records "the Father is greater than I" opens by calling the Word God (John 1:1, and on the earliest manuscripts, "only-begotten God" in 1:18) and closes with Thomas worshiping the risen Jesus as "my Lord and my God" — a confession Jesus accepts and blesses rather than corrects. If John were charting a gradual elevation of a mere rabbi, this is a strange way to write a book: framing the whole narrative with the highest possible confessions of Christ's deity while including, in between, sayings that reflect his voluntary humbling as true man. The more coherent reading — the one the Fathers used against real subordinationists — is that statements like John 14:28 speak κατ᾽ οἰκονομίαν (according to the incarnate mission), while statements like John 1:1, John 1:18, and John 20:28 speak κατ᾽ οὐσίαν (according to his eternal nature). The pattern isn't evolution toward deity; it's one Gospel holding together, without contradiction, the true God who became true man and thereby could, as man, call his Father greater.

transcript.content: You're right that *John 14:28* says exactly that: "The Father is greater than I." And in John 17:3 Jesus prays, "Now this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent." If Jesus really believed he was fully God—coequal with the Father—why would he say the Father is *greater*, and why distinguish himself from "the only true God"? The most natural reading is that here we have a subordinationist view: Jesus is exalted, honored, sent by God, but not God himself in the same way. That's precisely what *you'd* expect if an early Jewish movement gradually elevated a rabbi over decades, rather than what *you'd* expect if the incarnate God himself taught it from the start.
